speaker: RJ Scaringe
title: How to build a $16B car company with RJ Scaringe, founder of Rivian
question: In the automotive industry, why does selling direct-to-consumer matter far beyond eliminating the dealer sales commission?
guest: Selling through distributors and dealers often draws attention to the sale, saying you're paying a third party ten to fifteen percent to sell your car. That's true—that's a far less efficient way to sell the vehicle than having a direct relationship. But the unappreciated part is you lose out on all the business that happens post-sale. The service business actually becomes a very large part of revenue generation. If you look at large car dealer groups, they're very profitable, and where they make the vast majority of their money is on service. The thing you have to wrap your head around, though, is in the beginning, service is not a profitable business because you're investing a very large amount in building capacity—service infrastructure, a ton of CapEx, and a large team of service technicians. In the beginning, you're just performing warranty work; you don't really have paying service yet. Suddenly it goes from being a cost center—feeding in as warranty expense or OpEx—to profitable COGS, like an afterburner to the business once the car park is big enough to throw off billions of dollars a year in profit.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Direct-to-consumer sales matter because the dealer margin is only the visible part of what the franchise model costs an automaker. The larger prize is control over the whole business system.

First, the manufacturer owns the customer relationship and the data. That lets it sell high-margin software, subscriptions, insurance, financing, charging and over-the-air upgrades across the vehicle's life, rather than handing the customer to a dealer after the wholesale transaction.

Second, it controls pricing. Uniform, transparent prices end intra-brand discounting between dealers, protect brand value and residuals, and let the maker adjust prices instantly, as Tesla does.

Third, it changes inventory economics. Build-to-order or centrally pooled stock replaces weeks of vehicles sitting on dealer lots, cutting working capital, floorplan financing and the incentives needed to clear mismatched stock.

Fourth, it shifts the service model. Dealers earn most of their profit from parts, service and finance, which gives them weak incentives to push EVs that need less maintenance; a direct seller can design for low service and capture the remaining aftersales revenue itself.

The trade-off is that the manufacturer absorbs inventory risk, retail capital costs and legal fights over state franchise laws.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Selling direct-to-consumer transforms an automaker’s entire business model, shifting its role from a wholesale manufacturer whose actual customer is the dealership to an integrated technology and services company. Crucially, it resolves a structural incentive conflict: traditional franchise dealers earn the bulk of their profits from parts and maintenance, making them naturally reluctant to champion low-maintenance electric vehicles. Controlling retail ensures knowledgeable brand advocacy while replacing adversarial haggling and arbitrary markups with transparent, uniform pricing.

Equally important, direct sales give automakers end-to-end ownership of the customer relationship and first-party data, unlocking high-margin, recurring lifecycle revenue from over-the-air software upgrades, subscriptions, financing, insurance, and charging. Operationally, bypassing thousands of fragmented dealer lots enables centralized distribution and build-to-order manufacturing, slashing working capital, floorplan financing costs, and margin-eroding clearance incentives. Finally, owning the transaction gives manufacturers real-time pricing agility, allowing them to adjust prices dynamically to steer demand and match factory utilization with supply chain conditions.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Going direct-to-consumer changes how the whole business works, not just who collects the commission. First, the automaker owns the customer relationship and the data. It learns who buys what and why, and that feeds product planning, pricing and marketing. Second, it controls price. Fixed, transparent pricing removes haggling and stops dealers from discounting in ways that hurt brand value. It also lets the company raise or cut prices nationwide overnight, as Tesla often does. Third, inventory and capital work differently. Build-to-order selling cuts the billions tied up in dealer lots and the incentives needed to clear unwanted stock, so production tracks real demand. Fourth, it opens up recurring revenue after the sale. Software updates, subscriptions, insurance, financing, charging and service can all be sold directly over the car's life. Traditionally, dealers captured most of the parts, service and finance profit. Finally, the company controls the brand experience from start to finish. That's why franchise laws in many US states fight to block it, and why legacy automakers find the switch so hard.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Selling direct-to-consumer reshapes an automaker’s entire business model, not just its sales margin. First, it gives manufacturers direct ownership of the customer relationship and first-party data, enabling personalized engagement, faster product feedback, and tighter control over the brand experience. Without independent dealers adding markups or heavy discounts, automakers can maintain transparent, consistent pricing that protects brand equity and residual values. Operationally, direct sales let companies match production to real-time demand through centralized or build-to-order inventory, reducing overproduction, carrying costs, and reliance on dealer incentives. Just as important, it lets automakers capture high-margin lifetime revenue that dealers traditionally controlled—including financing, insurance, used-vehicle trade-ins, service, and recurring over-the-air software subscriptions. Finally, direct distribution eliminates incentive conflicts, which is especially critical for electric vehicles: traditional dealers earn heavily from combustion-engine maintenance and often resist pushing EVs, whereas a direct model aligns sales, software, and service around the manufacturer’s long-term strategy.

Selling direct gives an automaker control over the customer relationship. It can set the price buyers actually see, make ordering and delivery consistent, and learn firsthand which features people want and where they abandon a purchase. That feedback can shape product design, production, and inventory decisions.

The relationship also continues after delivery. The automaker has a direct channel for service, software upgrades, trade-ins, and the customer’s next purchase. It also takes on work dealers traditionally handle, including test drives, delivery, and local service. The strategic payoff is the ability to shape the entire ownership experience and use what it learns to earn repeat business.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra

Selling direct gives an automaker control over pricing and the customer relationship long after the car leaves the factory. When buyers configure and order cars directly, the manufacturer can see which features people want and what they’ll pay for, without having to infer demand from dealer orders. That can help it plan production, carry less inventory, and rely less on discounts to move unsold cars.

The relationship also continues after delivery. The automaker can use owner feedback to improve the car, sell software upgrades and services, and earn the owner’s next purchase. It takes on retail costs that dealers would otherwise bear, so the strategic payoff depends less on the margin from one sale than on what the automaker can learn and earn over years of ownership.
